documents.unit: Office of the Dean of Students
documents.title: Guidance on Preventing and Identifying Unauthorized Artificial Intelligence Usage
documents.summary: Faculty-facing guidance from the Dean of Students that ties unauthorized AI use to the Honor Code and tells instructors how to prevent it (syllabus statements, discussion, assignment prompts, proctoring) and how to identify and handle it (empathy, a conversation, caution with detectors, drafts and citation checks). It sets no AI permissions itself and leaves them to faculty syllabus statements.
documents.stance_why: The document gives advice to faculty and does not itself allow or ban AI: it says to 'Ensure that your syllabus contains a statement relating to the Honor Code and permissions regarding the usage of artificial intelligence (AI)'. Permissions are left to each instructor's statement and there are no tiers or templates, so the stance is delegates.

units.why: The guide opens by invoking the Honor Code Charter, which says work students submit is 'expected to be of their own creation'; that is an own-work rule binding students, so P29 (students own what they submit), with modality 'must' as an expectation.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P29, student, must, general. They differed on unit_stance (A neutral, B restrict) and on the normalized policy (A wrote one, B anchor-only). The source quotes the Honor Code Charter's own-work rule and does not mention AI in that sentence, so unit_stance is neutral; the sentence adds 'give proper credit', which A's policy keeps and the anchor omits.
units.anchor: all work that students submit is expected to be of their own creation
units.frag_start: According to the Honor Code Charter
units.policy: All work that students submit is expected to be of their own creation and give proper credit to the ideas and work of other individuals and resources.
units.fit_note: The passage also requires proper credit to others' ideas and work, which P29 does not capture.

units.why: The sentence states the guide's purpose: to guide faculty on preventing and identifying 'unauthorized artificial intelligence usage' in coursework. It sets the scope of the guidance, so P56 (framework stating purpose and scope) fits; it is addressed to instructors and is a statement of scope (informs).
units.resolution_why: Actor differed (A instructor, B admin). The source says the guide is 'meant to guide faculty', so it is addressed to faculty; actor is instructor. Type P56 and informs agreed.
units.anchor: guide faculty on both preventing unauthorized artificial intelligence usage and identifying
units.frag_start: This guide is meant
units.fit_note: Scope is limited to faculty guidance on prevention and identification, not an institution-wide framework of principles.

units.why: The text says AI tools 'may be used, whether intentionally or inadvertently, to develop and submit work that is not students' own' and that submitting one's own work is 'essential'. This gives the reason for the guidance: AI makes it easy to submit work that is not one's own, so P41 is nearest, though it is about integrity more than skill-building.
units.resolution_why: Actor differed (A all, B student). The sentence reads 'It is essential for students to develop and submit their own work', addressed to students, so actor is student. P41 with the shared fit_note.
units.anchor: It is essential for students to develop and submit their own work
units.frag_start: It is essential for students
units.fit_note: Rationale is that students must meet curricular goals through their own work; it does not argue that AI undermines practice or skill-building explicitly. Rationale is about meeting curricular goals by submitting own work, not explicitly about practice building skill.

units.why: Says easier access to AI tools may be used 'whether intentionally or inadvertently' to submit work not the student's own; context-setting problem statement, informs. No type fits a background statement that misuse may be inadvertent, so UNCOVERED.
units.resolution_why: Found only by coder B. The source says AI tools 'may be used, whether intentionally or inadvertently, to develop and submit work that is not students' own', a real statement of background that misuse can be inadvertent. Coder A did not code it. Kept as UNCOVERED, as B coded it, because no type covers a statement about inadvertent misuse.
units.anchor: whether intentionally or inadvertently, to develop and submit work that is not students’ own
units.frag_start: At the same time, access to generative
units.uncovered_note: States that AI misuse may be intentional or inadvertent as background to the guidance, without setting a rule.

units.why: Faculty are told to 'Ensure that your syllabus contains a statement relating to the Honor Code and permissions regarding the usage of artificial intelligence'. That is an instruction to include an AI statement in the syllabus, so P09 with modality 'should' (framed as a tip) addressed to instructors.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P09 and instructor but differed on phase (A before-course, B course-start) and modality (A should, B must). The source lists 'Ensure that your syllabus contains a statement...' under 'Those tips include', so it is advice, not a mandate: should. The syllabus statement is how expectations are communicated at the start of the course, so course-start.
units.anchor: Ensure that your syllabus contains a statement relating to the Honor Code and permissions
units.frag_start: Ensure that your syllabus
units.policy: Faculty ensure that the syllabus contains a statement relating to the Honor Code and permissions regarding the usage of artificial intelligence (AI).

units.why: Faculty are pointed to a collection of sample syllabus statements by discipline. It is a pointer to help instructors write their statements, which is support for faculty in setting policy, nearest P63 (support faculty in learning AI) though it is sample statements, not workshops.
units.resolution_why: Policy type differed (A P63 support faculty, B P09). The source points faculty to 'sample syllabi statements' directly under the heading 'Develop a Clear Syllabus Statement'. It helps write the syllabus statement and offers no training or consultation, so P09, as B coded it.
units.anchor: has collected sample syllabi statements for Generative AI tools by discipline
units.frag_start: Education Developer, Dr. Lance Eaton
units.policy: Faculty are directed to a collection of sample syllabus statements for generative AI tools by discipline.
units.fit_note: Offers sample statements as a resource rather than requiring one.

units.why: The guide recommends discussing 'the implications of AI misuse in the subject and potential career fields' at the start of the course, going beyond the syllabus. Explaining and discussing AI rules with students is exactly P66; it is timed at course start and uses 'can be beneficial', hence 'should'.
units.resolution_why: Coder B coded two P66 units (one per sentence of the dialogue tip) where A coded one. Both sentences make the same recommendation ('Going beyond the syllabus statement ... can be beneficial'; discuss AI misuse at the start of the course), so they are merged into one unit and B's second unit is dropped as a repeat. unit_stance differed (A neutral, B encourage); the unit encourages discussion of misuse and ethics, not AI use, so neutral.
units.anchor: At the beginning of your course, discussing the implications of AI misuse
units.frag_start: Going beyond the syllabus statement
units.policy: Faculty discuss the implications of AI misuse in the subject and in potential career fields at the beginning of the course, going beyond the syllabus statement.

units.why: Assignment prompts 'should include specific parameters for AI usage', especially for written work. This asks instructors to state AI rules in assignment instructions, matching P09, which includes assignment instructions.
units.anchor: should include specific parameters for AI usage
units.frag_start: Assignment prompts, especially for papers
units.policy: Assignment prompts, especially for papers or other written assessments, should include specific parameters for AI usage.

units.why: The sentence says specific prompts 'can help deter and detect unauthorized tool use'. It gives a prevention rationale for assignment-level AI parameters; best fit is P35 (redesign assignments around AI), since the rule is about how assignments are written.
units.anchor: Specific prompts can help deter and detect unauthorized tool use
units.frag_start: Specific prompts can help deter
units.policy: Specific assignment prompts can help deter and detect unauthorized tool use.
units.fit_note: Assignment wording is used as a deterrent and detection aid; no grading or structure change.

units.why: The charter now lets faculty proctor in-person exams, 'permitted, but not required', and a faculty presence 'can help ... deter academic integrity issues'. It concerns the exam environment, so nearest is P33 (shift toward proctored assessment), though it is optional, not a shift.
units.anchor: faculty are now permitted, but not required, to proctor in-person examinations
units.frag_start: Under the revised Honor Code charter
units.policy: Under the revised Honor Code charter, faculty are now permitted, but not required, to proctor in-person examinations.
units.fit_note: Proctoring is optional and framed as deterrence; the text does not say assessment weight shifts or that AI is banned in exams. Proctoring is optional for faculty rather than a required shift of weight to proctored assessment.

units.why: The guide says a supportive faculty presence 'can help serve as a resource to students' and deter integrity issues. This rationale for proctoring is a deterrence argument, not a rule on AI use, so UNCOVERED rather than stretched.
units.resolution_why: Policy type differed (A UNCOVERED, B P33). The source says 'A supportive faculty presence can help serve as a resource to students in the class and deter academic integrity issues': a rationale that presence deters integrity problems and helps students. P33 is a shift toward proctored assessment, which this sentence does not say, and the proctoring permission itself is already coded as P33. Prefer UNCOVERED over a stretched fit.
units.anchor: A supportive faculty presence can help serve as a resource to students
units.frag_start: A supportive faculty presence can
units.policy: A supportive faculty presence can help serve as a resource to students in the class and deter academic integrity issues.
units.uncovered_note: Rationale that instructor presence during in-person exams deters integrity violations and serves students as a resource.

units.why: Advice to 'Use Empathy' notes that confrontation is stressful and suggests framing the first inquiry around educational growth, with sample wording. This is a response to suspected misuse that is educative and not punitive, so P68; modality 'should' because it is advice.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P68, should, when-misuse. unit_stance differed (A neutral, B encourage); the advice is about how to frame an inquiry, not about AI use, so neutral.
units.anchor: Consider framing your initial inquiry in terms of educational growth
units.frag_start: Consider framing your initial inquiry
units.policy: Faculty consider framing their initial inquiry about suspected AI misuse in terms of educational growth.

units.why: The guide reports that 'Students have reported increased stress regarding potential false or wrongful accusations' about AI misuse, using it to justify empathy. It is a fact motivating fair handling, nearest P68 (reduce pressures and presume good faith), informs only.
units.anchor: Students have reported increased stress regarding potential false or wrongful accusations
units.frag_start: Students have reported increased stress
units.fit_note: Gives evidence of student stress about false accusations rather than prescribing an educative response.

units.why: During the meeting faculty should 'ask questions regarding the course content to assess if they understand the course content'. Checking understanding through a conversation with the student is P34.
units.anchor: ask questions regarding the course content to assess if they understand
units.frag_start: During your meeting with the student
units.policy: During the meeting with the student about the issue, faculty ask questions regarding the course content to assess whether the student understands the course content.

units.why: The advice 'Be Transparent' says to disclose the information that led to the suspicion to the student and point to questionable areas of the submitted work. That is open handling with the student before any escalation, so P57 (talk with the student first); fit is partial as it also concerns sharing the basis of suspicion.
units.anchor: Addressing the issue with transparency about your suspicion
units.frag_start: Addressing the issue with transparency
units.policy: Faculty address suspected unauthorized AI use with transparency about the suspicion, pointing to questionable areas of submitted work.
units.fit_note: Emphasizes disclosing the basis of the suspicion to the student, which P57 (talk first, gather context) does not state. Concerns instructors sharing the basis for suspicion with the student, closer to fairness and transparency than to pre-escalation conversation.

units.why: Faculty are told to 'ask to see versions from their drafting process' and to ask about working methods. Reviewing drafts is process evidence used to identify misuse, P40.
units.anchor: Ask the student about their working methods and ask to see versions
units.frag_start: Ask the student about their working
units.policy: Faculty ask the student about their working methods and ask to see versions from their drafting process.
units.fit_note: Process evidence is requested from the student in a conversation, not from software or logs.

units.why: States AI detection tools 'are not completely reliable and have shown bias', and not to overstate their reliability; reliability caution on detectors, P39.
units.anchor: AI detection tools are not completely reliable and have shown bias
units.frag_start: AI detection tools are not completely
units.policy: AI detection tools are not completely reliable and have shown bias through their responses.
units.fit_note: Detectors are not banned; they may help point to identifiers but cannot be proof alone.

units.why: The text says detector results 'alone cannot constitute a preponderance of evidence that AI was misused'. That sets an evidence standard for misuse findings, P69; it also limits reliance on detectors (P39 states unreliability separately).
units.anchor: their results alone cannot constitute a preponderance of evidence that AI was misused
units.frag_start: While these tools can help point out
units.policy: Detection tool results alone cannot constitute a preponderance of evidence that AI was misused.

units.why: The same passage says detectors 'can help point out certain identifiers of AI usage', so they may be used as one input. That is use of detection tools to identify misuse, P40, with caution.
units.resolution_why: Found only by coder A. The source says 'these tools can help point out certain identifiers of AI usage', a permitted, cautious use of detectors. It is a real statement distinct from the unreliability (P39) and evidence-standard (P69) units in the same passage. Kept.
units.anchor: these tools can help point out certain identifiers of AI usage
units.frag_start: While these tools can help point
units.fit_note: Permits detector use only as one cautious indicator, not as proof.

units.why: 'Check Citations' tells faculty that AI often generates wrong links or hallucinated citations and that ChatGPT leaves 'utm_source=chatgpt.com' in URLs. It names concrete evidence for identifying AI use, P40.
units.anchor: ChatGPT leaves a remnant in the URL hyperlink in papers
units.frag_start: Often, AI can generate wrong links
units.policy: Faculty check citations because AI can generate wrong links or hallucinate citations, and ChatGPT leaves a remnant in the URL hyperlink (utm_source=chatgpt.com).
units.fit_note: Identification relies on AI-generated artifacts in the submitted text, not on software, commit history or logs.

units.why: The guide advises checking 'inconsistencies between a student's writing' across assignments as a sign of possible misuse. Comparing work is process or similarity evidence for identifying misuse, P40.
units.resolution_why: Modality differed (A may, B should). The source says inconsistencies 'can help point to potential technology misuse', a possibility, not an instruction: may.
units.anchor: can help point to potential technology misuse
units.frag_start: Checking for inconsistencies between a student
units.policy: Checking for inconsistencies between a student's writing, either in one assignment or multiple, can help point to potential technology misuse.
units.fit_note: Stylistic comparison across submissions, not software or logs.

units.why: It cautions faculty to be 'cautious when confronting improvements in performance', because improvement is desirable. This limits what counts as evidence of misuse, which is P69.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P69, should, when-misuse. unit_stance differed (A neutral, B restrict). The warning concerns not over-reading improvement as misuse; it does not restrict AI use, so neutral.
units.anchor: be cautious when confronting improvements in performance through a course
units.frag_start: However, be cautious when confronting
units.policy: Faculty be cautious when confronting improvements in performance through a course, as improvement is a desirable outcome of good teaching and good efforts to learn.

units.why: Faculty are told asking students to write wholly in a Google Document 'can be a helpful way to view version history'. Version history is process evidence of misuse, P40; it also shapes how assignments are done.
units.anchor: Asking students to write assignments completely in a Google Document
units.frag_start: Asking students to write assignments completely
units.policy: Asking students to write assignments completely in a Google Document can be a helpful way to view version history to assess any suspicious text sections.
units.fit_note: The step is taken at assignment design time so version history exists, not only after suspicion.

units.why: Handwritten assignments, in part or in full, 'can help to focus students' attention and reduce overreliance on electronic resources'. This suggests changing assignment format in response to AI, P35.
units.anchor: can help to focus students’ attention and reduce overreliance on electronic resources
units.frag_start: whether in part or in full
units.policy: Handwritten assignments, whether in part or in full, can help to focus students' attention and reduce overreliance on electronic resources.

units.why: Faculty are invited to consult the Faculty or Student Honor Committee or the Honor System Liaison before or after talking with the student. This is a human support channel for instructors in suspected cases; no type covers instructor-facing consultation on integrity cases (P72 is for students, P63 is for learning AI).
units.anchor: feel free to consult with the Honor Committee
units.frag_start: If you have questions, either before or after
units.policy: Faculty may consult the Faculty Honor Committee, the Student Honor Committee, or the Honor System Liaison with questions before or after the initial conversation with the student.
units.uncovered_note: Instructors may consult the Honor Committee or the Honor System Liaison about suspected AI misuse.

notes: Single university-layer document (Dean of Students AI guidance). The Honor Code Charter (AI unauthorized unless faculty specify) is not in the saved text, so it is not coded. Several P40/P69 units split one detection passage into distinct rules. Reconciled from two coders; see resolution_why on units.
